newsitem.title: CHINA: Inter-Korean Red Cross talks on food aid adjourned.
newsitem.headline: Inter-Korean Red Cross talks on food aid adjourned.

text.p: The first inter-Korean Red Cross talks in almost five years was adjourned in Beijing on Saturday with no agreement on speeding up food aid to the hungry North.
Lee Byung-woong, secretary general of South Korea's Red Cross, said he expected "good results" when the talks resume in the Chinese capital on Monday.

The North is sliding into a famine after the Stalinist hermit nation was hit by devastating floods for two years in a row. Red Cross officials have said the Beijing talks would focus on procedures for transporting and distributing food for the North, but not the size or timing of aid.
At the talks, the South sought "fast and efficient delivery" of food aid to the North to cut cost and delivery time, Lee told a news conference, but he declined to give details.
Red Cross officials have said Seoul would propose delivering food aid through the Korean border village of Panmunjom, instead of the present methods of using ships or trains through China.
The South also wanted to hand over aid directly to the North instead of through the International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies, Red Cross officials have said.
The last inter-Korean Red Cross talks were held in August, 1992, in Panmunjom, the only border crossing point between the two Koreas.
International aid groups say North Korea is sliding into famine with reported deaths of children from malnutrition and farmers eating powdered wood to fill out their diet.
"During the last two months, the situation has gone from bad to worse," Ole Gronning, International Federation of Red Cross representative in North Korea, told Reuters in an interview.

"The stocks are now completely empty. So if we don't get considerable support from outside here and now, we are facing a large-scale humanitarian disaster in North Korea with massive starvation," he said.
North Korea has said its food supplies would run out at the end of April.
The U.N. World Food Programme estimated there was only enough food to feed the country until June and then its 24 million people would have to wait for the next harvest in October and November.
South Korea, the United States and Japan are scheduled to hold talks in Tokyo on May 7 to discuss food shortages in the North and ways to encourage Pyonyang to join peace talks.
Seoul, Washington and Tokyo are worried that a desperate North Korean leadership might strike the South if an economic crisis threatened its survival.
Peace talks involving the two Koreas, the United States and China, are aimed at closing the book on the 1950-53 Korean War, which ended in a now-fraying armistice.
North Korea last month agreed to join four-nation peace talks if it was first guaranteed large-scale food aid, U.S. diplomatic recognition and an easing of trade sanctions.
The United States has pledged $25 million and South Korea $6 million to the World Food Programme, which has appealed for $95.5 million to provide 203,000 tonnes of food to North Korea.
South Korea has said it was considering sending an additional 50,000 tonnes of corn.

Japan has held back food aid, partly due to anger over charges that North Korea kidnapped a Japanese schoolgirl in 1977 and spirited her to Pyongyang. The United States has said it would not press Japan to donate more food aid to North Korea.
